Phantom pain

By: Jason Boswell | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
A local researcher is leading the fight against phantom pain

Unique Selling Point:
Kathlego Limakatso is a physiotherapist is conducting a trial using a new technique, Graded Motor Imagery, for the first time in Africa to relieve phantom pain caused by amputations with virtually a 100% success rate.

Summary:
For years phantom pain was poorly understood and was treated using mirror therapy. However, this technique proved to only reduce pain by approximately 20%-30%; Kathlego's trial using Graded Motor Imagery - which involved teach patients a variety of techniques through the use of a free app has helped improved the pain reduction to 100% in virtually of of his test subjects. This is the first time this method is being trialled in Africa. Limakatso has already won an award for his work. The patients are based out of Khayelitsha, Somerset West and Victoria Hospitals. According to Limakatso the therapies are cheap and able to be performed anywhere which opens them up to a much larger portion of the population, rather than just those who can afford private medical aid cover.

Eileen is one of his patients, from Somerset West, who described the sensation of phantom pain in her left as feeling like, "broken glass under her skin". After her amputation, due to diabetes, she couldn't sleep and was taking vast quantities of pain killers and sleeping tablets to simply be able to function. According to her pre-admission study her pain was rated as 9/10 using a universal medical pain scale. This rating means the pain is so severe it disables the patient and they are unable to perform "activities of daily living". Eileen says she is now totally pain free and says the treatment saved her life and she can live normally now and go back to work as a booking's agent for a cage-diving company.

Limakatso says that after the success of this trial the team, including himself and several neuroscientists at Groote Schuur's Pain Management Unit want to roll this treatment method out to other sufferers of Chronic Complex Pain Syndrome which affects vastly more people.

Further information:
Both Katlego and Eileen have said they are available and willing to conduct the filming on a weekend.

I have also spoken with the other neuroscientists involved - one of whom is Kathlego's Master's supervisor - who would talk to us about the latest understanding of phantom pain and its mechanism and treatments.

We could also set up an additional case study should it be required.

Script:


Script Visuals
VO: Eileen McCausland, an Irish expat who made South Africa her home, was devastated when her leg was amputated because of complications due to diabetes…

As the traumatic pain of the amputation started to subside…she began suffering from an insidious condition, known as Phantom Pain, a little understood phenomenon where amputees feel excruciating pain sensations, where their missing limbs used to…
Wide shots of Eileen driving and walking into her house…

Eileen McClausland, “It’s like if you get drilled by the dentist…It’s not there…”



For Eileen the pain was debilitating and she could no longer enjoy her active life where participating in Tai Chi and Pole Dancing classes… or just simple everyday things like walking her dog…and the constant unwaivering pain began to take its toll…




Eileen McCausland “Nothing took the pain away…The worst thing that’s ever happened to me in my life…”
VO: As lifestyle diseases such as diabetes become more prominent across every level of South African society the number of amputations, and people affected by pain associated with them, will inevitably increase…






Wide shots of Groote Schuur, general hospital shots….
Claire Mawisa link
VO: Romy Parker is President of PainSA, a group of professionals from various disciplines focussed on how best addressing pain management and education on treatment methods across the country…
Romy Set ups…
Romy Parker “Phantom Limb pain occurs when…That’s not even there anymore…”
VO: The brain is a notoriously intricate organ and the exact mechanism of phantom pain is still not yet fully understood…

Functional MRI scans of patients with phantom pain show that neural activity in the areas of the brain associated with limb recognition differ from patients without the condition…

The way the brain maps out various parts of the body in order to recognise them has been altered…It is this disconnect that causes the brain create the experience of pain…
Graphic sequence
Romy Parker “Understanding that pain is about the brain….So you can start getting your life back…” Interview and cutaways
Link about amputations affect up to 85% of amputees in Katleho…
V/O Mirror therapy has been used extensively over the past two decades to treat phantom pain by teaching patients to discern between their left and right limbs after amputation….however, according to a new study the effectiveness of this treatment was erratic…

Katleho Limakatso, a pain researcher from the University of Cape Town became fascinated with phantom pain during his student years and is now at the forefront of its treament…



Mirror therapy image sequence




Katleho set up sequence walking into hospital…(laptop image with brain MRI scan on)
Katleho Limakatso “Pain is a real thing, you don’t imagine it…We need to address those changes to deal with the pain…”
Katleho, along with Romy, co-authored a new study using a technique called Graded Motor Imagery which has been used to treat other chronic pain conditions but this is the first time it’s been trialled with Phantom Pain in Africa.

In Graded Motor Imagery patients use a sequential three part technique that allows the damaged neurological map of the brain to methodically be rewired, basically the technique teaches the patients to use, or create, new neural pathways so the brain can send and receive information along new routes.

In this study patients are first taught to RE-recognise left and right in the amputated limbs using either an app on a smart phone or images in a magazine or newspaper.

Then move onto imagining moving their lost limb independently before finally moving onto traditional mirror therapy…the researchers believe that introducing the two initial steps help the brain remap the pathways more effectively and thus improve the overall effectiveness of the pain relief…


Dumisani Mafilika lost his leg after stepping on broken glass in Khayelitsha and contracting a life-threatening infection…

For him, the phantom pain was so excruitating he was at times not able to eat or help himself around the house…But now after Katleho has introduced him to Graded Motor Imagery, his situation has improved…
Treatment images – app, movements, mirrors…
Dumisani Mafilika, “ When I look at that mirror, it is as though, (the movement) is performed by the absent limb….So even the pain disappears and it is as though the missing leg is moving.

Claire Question into Katleho answer about the effectiveness of the study…
Katleho Limakatso “We determined the effectiveness of the treatment…We had great success across the board…”
V/O While the intial results have been encouraging from a scientific point of view, for these patients and their families… the effect on their quality of life is far more important… Dumisani in Khayelitsha, sister helping with tea
Phelokazi Mafilika, “ When I look at that mirror, it is as though, (the movement) is performed by the absent limb….So even the pain disappears and it is as though the missing leg is moving.

VO: Amputations affect every level of South African society whether it be from trauma or lifestyle diseases…

In future, Katleho and the team are hoping to roll out the use of Graded Motor Imagery not only in the educational curricuculum for health professionals involved in pain treatment but also to help educate the public about the causes of pain and different treatment options…
(maybe have a short sequence of Eileen and Dumisani running as a split screen?)

Katleho in front of computer going through pain study sequence and book shelves…
Katleho Limakatso “Some of the patients I’ve came across…This is the treatment to effectively treat it…”








Eileen’s pain level from phantom pain was the single highest recorded for any patient before going into treatment with the study…scoring 9 out of a possible 10 on the universal medical pain scale…the pain also resulted in her becoming depressed, however, the results of the trial have been life-changing… Eileen reading, playing with dog or at work…
Eileen McCausland “I think it’s a miracle…I would never gotten out of that dark hole…”





Promos
10 second VO:

Feeling pain in a limb that’s not there? That’s the terrible reality for up to 85% of amputees, but new science could lead to better treatment of this strange condition…
15 seconder #1

It’s one of the most puzzling medical mysteries where amputees, can still feel pain, at the site of the missing limb.
Eileen UPSOUND

Now new research, has been developed to help treat this condition…
15 seconder #2

This young South African researcher is on the forefront of the fight against phantom pain…a poorly understood and bizarre condition that affects amputees…

Katleho UPSOUND…
